unit.name: Trends after LLM application engineering
unit.description: Wraps up the lecture with a recap and forward-looking discussion of scaling plateaus, architecture search, multimodality, hybrid learning methods, human-inspired versus non-human-inspired approaches, and skill half-life.
unit.summary: The recap lists the major LLM optimization levers covered in the lecture: better prompts, chains, fine-tuning, retrieval, and multi-agent systems [ts=6185s]. The instructor then raises the open question of whether LLMs are plateauing, noting that scaling laws suggest improvement from more compute and energy but that new architectures may be needed for the next step [ts=6220s]. Architecture search is positioned as a possible path to a next-transformer-style breakthrough that reduces compute or energy needs [ts=6272s]. Multimodality is presented as another trend: adding vision, audio, and video can improve the whole model, not only the added modality [ts=6356s]. The lecture also argues that future systems may combine supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, reinforcement learning, prompt engineering, and RAG in harmony, while research explores both human-inspired and non-human-inspired approaches [ts=6413s]. The final lesson is breadth-first learning because individual RAG or agent techniques change quickly and the half-life of specific skills is short [ts=6542s].

key_points.text: The lecture recaps prompts, chains, fine-tuning, retrieval, and multi-agent systems as LLM optimization techniques.
The plateau question asks whether future LLMs will improve as quickly as past generations.
Scaling laws imply more compute and energy can continue to improve LLMs, but eventual plateaus motivate architecture search.
Architecture search could produce a next-transformer-style breakthrough that reduces compute or energy by an order of magnitude.
Adding modalities such as images, audio, and video can improve the model's overall understanding across modalities.
Future systems may combine supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, reinforcement learning, prompt engineering, and RAG.
Because AI techniques change fast, the course prioritizes breadth and the ability to go deep when needed.
